tasks.q: What does a software licence set out?
a: What you are allowed to do with the program
Which language it was written in
tasks.fb: Use, copy, modify, distribute: the four questions every licence answers.

tasks.q: You buy a copy of a design program. What have you bought?
a: A licence to use it under the terms set by the publisher
tasks.fb: Which is why installing it on twenty machines may breach the licence.

tasks.q: What is the defining feature of proprietary software?
a: The source code is not made available, so users cannot change it
It cannot be copied at all
tasks.fb: Some proprietary software is free to use; the code is still closed.

tasks.q: Why might a hospital choose proprietary software?
a: It comes with a support contract and someone accountable when it fails
tasks.fb: When the system matters, someone to call at 3am is worth paying for.

tasks.q: What is the defining feature of open source software?
a: The source code is available, so it can be studied and modified
tasks.fb: Open source is about the code being open, not simply about price.

tasks.q: Which are genuine advantages of open source software? Select all that apply.
opts: It can be adapted to exactly what you need
Many developers can inspect the code for faults
It is always easier to use
correct: It can be adapted to exactly what you need
Many developers can inspect the code for faults
tasks.fb: Open code is inspected more, but inspection is not a guarantee.

tasks.q: Does each statement describe open source or proprietary software?
items: The source code is kept secret
Users may adapt it to their needs
Support comes with the licence fee
Support may rely on forums and volunteers
Usually paid for per user or machine
tasks.fb: Four rows of that table are the most common exam question in this lesson.

tasks.q: Why might free open source software still cost a school money?
a: It may need staff time or a paid contract to install, maintain and support it
tasks.fb: Total cost of ownership is the phrase the industry uses.

tasks.q: Match each situation to the more suitable licence type, based on the reason given.
pairs: A charity with technical volunteers and no budget
A hospital system needing a guaranteed response time
A university wanting to modify software for its own research
A small firm with no IT staff needing something that just works
tasks.fb: Budget, skills, criticality and the need to adapt decide it.

tasks.q: Which is the best exam answer for a school on a tight budget with a capable technician?
a: Open source, because there is no licence fee and the technician can adapt and maintain it
Open source, because it is free

info.title: Open source runs the internet
info.text: Most web servers, and the software behind most websites, are open source. So is the code inside most phones.

info.title: Licences differ
info.text: Some open source licences let you do almost anything; others require you to publish your changes. Reading the licence matters.

info.title: Paid open source
info.text: Companies sell supported versions of open source software: the code is free, the support contract is not.

info.title: Security both ways
info.text: Open code lets more people find flaws, including attackers. Closed code hides flaws from everyone, including defenders.

info.title: Schools and cost
info.text: Licensing is one of the largest lines in a school's IT budget, which is why the question comes up in real life as well as exams.

info.title: Lock-in
info.text: The cost of leaving a supplier, because your data and workflows are tied to their software, is called lock-in, and it is a real argument for open formats.
